subsection.title: Why the converse is false
subsection.p: The theorem has only one direction. Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability.
Continuity says the graph has no break at the point. Differentiability says the graph has one limiting slope there. A graph can be unbroken and still have no single tangent slope.

exercise.title: Why does continuity not imply differentiability?

statement.p: Continuity is about nearby heights; differentiability is about nearby slopes. In your own words, why can a graph be unbroken and still fail to have a derivative, and how does |x| at 0 separate the two ideas?

hint.p: Nearby values can match while the left and right limiting slopes disagree. A corner is continuous but not locally linear.

note.title: Continuity and differentiability
note.p: Continuity requires nearby function values to approach the value at the point.
It does not imply that a finite tangent slope exists.

exercise.title: How can differentiability fail even when the graph does not jump?

statement.p: Corners, cusps, and vertical tangents all prevent a finite two-sided derivative, while a jump already prevents continuity. In your own words, what happens to nearby slopes in each of the first three cases, and why does continuity rule out only the fourth?

hint.p: A derivative requires one finite limiting slope. Finite-but-unequal, unbounded-in-opposite-directions, and unbounded-together are three different ways that demand can fail.

but there is no left side inside the domain. Later, endpoints will matter when we look for maximum and minimum values on closed intervals. At endpoints, one-sided behavior is useful, but it is not the same as the ordinary derivative.

The derivative is a strong demand. It gives continuity and a local linear model. The next question is practical: for the smooth functions we meet every day, how do we compute derivatives without returning to the limit definition each time?

exercise.title: Why is the ordinary derivative two-sided?

statement.p: The definition of f'(a) uses a two-sided limit, so f must be defined near a from both sides. In your own words, why does that prevent an ordinary derivative of \sqrt{x} at 0, even though a right-hand quotient can still be studied?

hint.p: At an endpoint there is no other side inside the domain. One-sided behavior is useful, but it is not the same as the two-sided derivative.
